content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the application of causal inference theory in offline reinforcement learning. The authors first provide a non-identifiability result showing that it is impossible to recover actual causal effects of treatment X on an outcome Y from the observational data alone, assuming underlying structural functions are linear and unobserved confounding generally exists. This impossibility result suggests that one must explore the causal relationships among variables for practical offline RL. The authors then provide a variation of PC, a well-celebrated causal discovery algorithm, to learn an equivalence class of causal graphs from the observational data while incorporating additional temporal constraints.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper is technically sound. The non-identifiability is not surprising and agrees with existing results in causal inference literature. The extension of PC algorithm to incorporate additional temporal constraints might benefit some researchers in the field.

As for the weakness, first, the main claim of this paper, "causal environment models can outperform plain environment models in offline RL", has been known. Indeed, it is part of the central claims of Pearl's causal hierarchy (Pearl & Mackenzie, 2018) since offline observational data lies in layer 1 and reinforcement learning lies in layer 2. It has been shown in the causal hierarchy theorem (Bareinboim, Correa, Ibeling & Icard, 2022) that data in a lower layer (observational) almost always underdetermines a query in a higher layer (experimental). The authors conclude Section 4 by showing the necessity of a causal environment model in offline RL. This result is not surprising and is expected from the existing literature. It would be appreciated if the authors could further elaborate Theorem 4.5, highlighting its novelty and contributions to the current literature. In its current form, it is a bit unclear how significant these results are.

Following the above point, several related references are missing. More recently, there is a growing line of work exploring the relation between causal inference and reinforcement learning  (Bareinboim et al., 2015; Forney et al., 2017; Zhang and Bareinboim, 2017; Lee and Bareinboim, 2018; Kallus and Zhou, 2018; Forney and Bareinboim, 2019; Lee and Bareinboim, 2019; Zhang and Bareinboim, 2019, 2020; Lee and Bareinboim, 2020b; Zhang et al., 2020; Namkoong et al., 2020; Etesami and Geiger, 2020; Kallus and Zhou, 2020; Zhang and Bareinboim, 2021a; Wang et al., 2021; Tennenholtz et al., 2021; Kumor et al., 2021; Zhang and Bareinboim, 2022; Ruan and Di, 2022). The connection between do-intervention and RL was first noted in (Bareinboim et al., NeurIPS 2015). The impossibility of inferring causal effects from data in offline RL with the presence of unobserved confounding (UC) was also discussed in (Zhang & Bareinboim, IJCAI 2017). To address the challenges of UCs,  (Kallus & Zhou, 2018; Namkoong et al., 2020; Zhang & Bareinboim 2021) applied the methods of partial identification to infer bounds over the actual causal effects from the observational data. (Zhang & Bareinboim, 2017, 2019, 2020) further utilized these bounds to accelerate a future online learning process. I would encourage the authors to include a comprehensive discussion on how this work is positioned in the current literature. This will help the readers to see how it adds to the state-of-art methods.

Finally, the choice of extending PC algorithm is curious. In section 4.1, the authors consider linear causal models where the spurious noise variables could be correlated. That is, unobserved confounding generally exists. However, PC algorithm is only applicable to Markovian models where all noise variables are independent and no UC exists. Since the spurious correlation among variables is presented as the main challenge of this paper, it is a bit odd that the authors somehow assume it away in the later section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity of this paper could be improved. It starts with the challenge of unobserved confounding (UC) in the offline data, and implicitly assumes this challenge away when introducing its main algorithm. It would be appreciated if the authors could explicitly explain and elaborate on the theoretical assumptions that underlie this paper. 

The theoretical results in this paper seem sound. However, as explained in previous points, some of the claims overlap with existing results in the literature. Therefore, the novelty of this paper might be somewhat limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper studies the application of causal inference theory in offline reinforcement learning. The authors provide an impossibility result showing the necessity of a causal environment model in offline RL when unobserved confounding (UC) exists. However, such a conclusion has been known in the literature. There is a growing number of work studying how to address the issues of non-identifiability. It would be appreciated if the authors could include a comprehensive discussion on how this paper is positioned in the current literature. Also, the proposed algorithm, FOCUS, extends PC and is only applicable to Markovian environments where UC does not exist. This assumption might be overly restrictive and assumes away the key challenge of this paper.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces causality to learn a more effective environment model for model-based reinforcement learning.  

They first provide some **theoretical proof, to clarify that the environment, learning with causal clues is much more helpful than the plain one. Second, they propose a new method, namely FOCUS, which modifies PC to achieve causality discovery more efficiently and trains an environment model by supervised learning.**

The experiments provide corroboration for their theory and methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength
    - The paper is well-organized.
    - The theoretical proof surely provides a good basis for the following work
    - The analysis and conclusion of how to choose conditional variable is well
- Weakness
    - They claim that they modify the PC algorithm. However, while involving causality in RL, only considering the causal relationship between the current step and the next step is a common way, as well as excluding the compound causality situation.
    - If I understand correctly, the FOCUS applies the PC algorithm to discover the causality graph within the environment and then takes it as a hard mask of state and action pair in supervised environment model learning. This way is not novel for me. Is there anything relating to the good theoretical proof to enhance the causal discovery, environment learning, or the policy learning process?  Are the two mentioned bounds, model prediction error bound and policy evaluation error bound involved in the FOCUS methods?
    - Besides, more details are required. For example,
        - how do the X_cau and X_spu work in FOCUS? Does FOCUS applies causal discovery to distinguish them, and then use them as the mask of input?
        - the definition of causal discovery metric is not clear. Especially in robustness, the paper mentioned variance but what is the variance for is unknown to the readers.
    - Some statements do not convince me. For example,
    - Could you please provide more analysis? like why FOCUS failed in CAR DRIVING but success in MUJOCO.
    - Some math symbols should be modified or clarified
        - like the X_spu, some sentences use X_spu, and others use \boldsymbol{X}_spu
        - what is the \sigma in Eq. 4. and what does the \independent denote? the independent relationship?
        - Besides, according to Table 1, all the methods except LNCM have the same-level efficiency, then all of them should be written in blod
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The clarity is clear, that the causal clues can be helpful in learning environment model.
- More details are required.
- For reproducibility, it is better to provide codes.
content.summary_of_the_review: A very good theoretical analysis is given, But the proposed method still has room for improvement.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This submission proposes incorporating ideas from causality into model based RL.  It includes a theoretical result (Theorem 4.5) that provides a bound on policy evaluation error when using a learned model in the presence of spurious features.  In this case, the spurious features areGiven by a linear transformation of the true causal features with some added zero-mean noise.  

It also proposes a method for learning a more causally correct environment model.  I was not able to understand how the method works or evaluate experimental results, due to major issues of clarity.  My understanding is that the method somehow uses causal independence testing to determine which dimensions of the current state and action cause which dimensions of the next state and action, and then builds an environment model that respects this causal structure.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The idea of incorporating causality into model-based RL is a good one.
- The results appear to demonstrate qualitative advantages of this approach.

Weaknesses:
- Insufficient clarity.
- There was not enough intuition provided for the theorem or its proof.
- The conclusion describes the experiments as “extensive” which is overstated; it is typical to evaluate on multiple Mujoco environments in offline RL.  In the Appendix, the authors note (If I understand correctly) that other Mujoco environments lack spurious features, and thus their algorithm would reduce to MOPO, but it would still be worth running the experiments there.  I'm not convinced that this would be the result; It seems like it would depend on p*.  It would also be easy to make versions of other Mujoco environments that include spurious features of the kind described in Section 4.1.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
I did not find the paper clear enough to understand or evaluate the method or experiments.  
- The “condition variable” is not defined as a general concept, and it is not stated which variables are considered the condition variable in the various experiments, so I was not able to determine what experiments were conducted, or how the method works.  
- It is not clear what assuming “Faithfulness in the environment transition” means in this context.  My understanding is that the Faithfulness condition means that a graph represents exactly the independence relations of the corresponding probability distribution, but no graph is provided for “the environment transition” -- e.g. Are different elements of the state considered as separate nodes?  Are there any arrows between them?  Are all the elements of the current state connected to all the elements of the next state?  Figure 9 provides some hints about this, but it seems there are no spurious features in the graph of the kind mentioned in Section 4.1 (which would correspond to arrows between elements of S_t)?  Why would the method help in such a case?  Is the theory applicable to this case?
- “The PC algorithm” is mentioned without any reference or definition.

Novelty: I have no reason to suspect this work is not novel.  It seems like a fairly straightforward application of puzzle independence testing to model-based RL, which might be low novelty, but still high significance if it hasn’t been done.

Quality: I was not able to evaluate the quality due to lack of clarity.

Reproducibility: i believe the description of the method and experiments are incomplete; see my comments on clarity.
content.summary_of_the_review: I did not find the paper clear enough to understand; it seems to lack critical details of the method and experiments.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
